Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "NeuroQuery: comprehensive meta-analysis of human brain mapping" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Christian Büchel as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Tor D. Wager (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

This paper describes NeuroQuery, a new approach to automated meta-analysis of the neuroimaging literature. It is demonstrably superior for many purposes – particularly as a starting point for constraining predictive models and as regions or patterns of interest in new studies. We believe that this will be a very widely used, and cited, tool. It's also a tremendous amount of work to build and validate, and very few groups have both the skills and motivation to build this and make it accessible to the broad neuroscience/neuroimaging community.

There are a number of exemplary features of this work, including:

– A full implementation that is openly shared on Github, including source code, models, and data

– A fully functional web interface that runs simply and beautifully

– Several types of validation of the model's performance, including (a) stability with rare terms listed in few studies, (b) reproducibility of maps with limited data, (c) better encoding/prediction of brain maps associated with terms.

This work dramatically expands the vocabulary of search terms that can be used in neuroimaging meta-analyses. We believe this is going to be really useful. The model framework is also interesting and motivated by some careful considerations in terms of how the model should be affected by certain classes of rare terms, features included in the model, etc. The bottom line for users is a better set of predictive maps. While there are many potential varieties of such models and one could second-guess some particular choices, the beauty of the authors' approach is that the code is available for others to try out variations and build/validate a different model based on their sensibilities and preferences.

Essential revisions:

1) We believe that the validations are insufficient for some of the claims. The authors should either expand their experiments to validate these claims or tone down their claims.

A) "NeuroQuery, can assemble results from the literature into a brain map based on an arbitrary query." This statement can be mis-interpreted to mean that users can enter any terms they want. My understanding is that the query has to comprise words from the 7547 dictionary words. Words outside the dictionary are ignored.

B) Introduction: "For example, some rare diseases, or a task involving a combination of mental processes that have been studied separately, but never – or rarely – together." This suggests NeuroQuery can do this with precision, but the authors have not experimentally demonstrated that activation maps involving "combination of mental processes that have been studied separately, but never together" can be accurately predicted. To validate this, the authors should consider cases involving compound mental processes (e.g., "auditory working memory") and remove all experiments involving both "auditory" + "working memory". Care has to be taken to also remove experiments using words similar to "auditory" + "working memory", so that experiments such as "auditory n-back" are also removed, even though the experiments did not explicitly use the term "working memory". Note that the entire experiments should be removed, rather than just the specific words. The authors can then re-train their model and show whether the query "auditory working memory" yields activation similar to the removed experiments involving auditory working memory.

C) For subsection “NeuroQuery can map rare or difficult concepts”, it's important to differentiate between a concept that is rarely studied versus a rare word that seldom appears in the literature even though variations of the word might be widely studied. The whole section seems to imply that the NeuroQuery is able to accomplish the former very well, but in the experiment, they chose frequent terms (e.g., language) and progressively delete them from their dataset, thus they are really testing the latter. To really test the former, rather than just deleting the word "language" from the documents, they should delete entire documents containing "language" and/or other terms similar to language (e.g., semantic).

2) Figure 8 (right panel) should be in the main text in addition to (or replacing) Figure 6. While the log likelihood measure is valid, the "absolute" measure is much more helpful to the users of knowing how much to trust the results. Along this note, it is somewhat concerning that the overall accuracy is only 70% – how much should a user trust a tool with a 70% accuracy? However, this is perhaps underselling NeuroQuery because coordinates tend to be sparse, so just based on the reported coordinates, this classification task might simply be very hard. What might be more useful would be for the user to get a sense of how much the NeuroQuery maps actually matches real activation maps. Can the authors perform the same experiment, but using real activation maps from NeuroVault or their own Individual Brain Charting dataset? This is just a suggestion. The authors can choose to just discuss this issue.

3) Results section: some pieces of argumentation presented here are not fully convincing. The authors propose that: "Term co-occurrences, on the other hand, are more consistent and reliable, and capture semantic relationships [Turney and Pantel, 2010]". Most of the brain mapping literature is made of attempts to differentiate cognitive processes inferred from the study of human behaviour such as "proactive control VS retroactive control", "recollection VS familiarity", "face perception VS place perception", "positive emotion VS negative emotion". In that context, it is unclear how terms co-occurrence for example between "face" and "place" would be more consistent and reliable than "face" alone. Term co-occurrence mainly reflects what type of concepts tend to be studied together.

4) The authors suggest that "It would require hundreds of studies to detect a peak activation pattern for "aphasia". It is not clear what do the authors mean here. Aphasia is a clinical construct referring to a behavioural disturbance. It is defined as "an inability (or impaired ability) to produce or understand speech". Accordingly, we don't see how one could search for a peak of activation related to aphasia? The line of argumentation could be clarified here by starting with concrete examples. Perhaps an example the authors may refer to is that, starting from a clinical point of view, researchers may want to investigate brain activation related to the processes of language production in order to better understand dysfunctions such those seen in aphasia. Accordingly, the related publication will probably mention "aphasia" "language production" "phonological output lexicon" etc… and this pattern of terms could in turn be linked to similar language related terms in other publications. An alternative guess is that maybe the authors actually refer here to lesion studies that have, for example, searched for correlation between grey matter volume atrophy and aphasia?

5) We have some suggestions for improving the Abstract/Introduction

A) Explaining how a predictive framework allows maps to be generated by generalizing from terms that are well studied ("faces") to those that are less well studied and inaccessible to traditional meta-analyses ("prosopagnosia"). And explaining that this is good for some use cases (generating sensible ROIs/making guesses about where future studies of prosopagnosia might activate), but not good for others (e.g., knowing that a particular area is (de)activated in studies of prosopagnosia).

B) Can you provide a bit more context on previous topic models (e.g., Nielsen/Hansen NNMF "bag of words" work from way back, Poldrack/Yarkoni topic models, GCLDA) and how this approach is different. After reading the Introduction, readers have a sense of what Neuroquery does (its goal), but not how it actually does it (no algorithmic insight). For example, Neuroquery "infers semantic similarities across terms used in the literature", but so does a topic model (which is not mentioned/cited). We recommend including more description early on of what the algorithmic differences are relative to previous work that confer advantages. This is explained later (with some redundancy across sections), but more up front would be helpful.

C) In the Introduction, the authors argue that meta-analyses are limited primarily by performance of in-sample statistical inference (they "model all studies asking the same question") and lack of use of a predictive framework. While there is great value in the current work, we don't think that is strictly true. Other meta-analyses have taken a predictive approach, in a limited way, and also modeled differences across study categories. The Naive Bayes classifier analyses in the Neurosynth paper (Yarkoni, 2011) are an example. And Neurosynth considers topics across tasks and fields of study. Analyzing studies by single search terms is an important limitation (topic models by Poldrack and Yarkoni help; perhaps acknowledge their 2014 paper). Viewing the paper as a whole, we understand why the authors focus on prediction vs. inference in the Introduction, but it's hard to understand how this other work fits in without having gone through the whole paper.

D) Likewise, the emphasis on the ability to interpolate struck us as odd. We understand this as generalizing based on semantic smoothing. This is useful, but we don't think what you meant was really clearly explained in the Introduction.

E) The authors make a compelling case that current meta-analyses are limited. The Pinho 2018 example is very helpful: An automated meta-analysis of all the studies performing the same or a similar contrast is not currently possible, primarily because we have lacked the tools to parse the natural language text in articles well enough to identify an "equivalence class" of functional contrasts.

F) "For example, some rare diseases, or a task involving a combination of mental processes that have been studied separately, but never – or rarely – together." Could the authors provide a concrete example?

6) We have some suggestions for improving the clarity of the Results section:

A) “NeuroQuery relies on a corpus of 13459 full-text neuroimaging publications”

What type of neuroimaging publications? task-based activations experiments? If so, of which type: PET and fMRI or only fMRI-based? does it also include structural MRI studies? does it include all types of populations (healthy adults, elderly, patients studies)?

B) It is not clear how to read Figure 1. What do the length and width of the color and grey lines represent? could this figure be more elaborated to integrate additional aspects of the procedure? e.g. each of the three brain slice has a color that seems to reflect their respective association with the term, how is all that information combine to a single brain pattern?

C) Terminological precision: Results paragraph one: the term "area" is usually reserved for brain territories defined based on microstructure features (e.g. Area 4). Here the authors refer to a spatial location in the brain (or maybe a zone of homogeneity with regards to a specific feature), so they should prefer the term "brain region" for that purpose.

D) Finally, the supplement material provides several quantitative evidence of significant improvement compared to Neurosynth, such as:

– "our method extracted false coordinates from fewer articles: 3 / 40 articles have at least one false location in our dataset, against 20 for NeuroSynth"

– "In terms of raw amount of text, this corpus is 20 times larger than NeuroSynth's"

– "Compared with NeuroSynth, NeuroQuery's extraction method reduced the number of articles with incorrect coordinates (false positives) by a factor of 7, and the number of articles with missing coordinates (false negatives) by a factor of 3 (Table 2)."

All these aspects could be summarized together with the more qualitative aspects in a table to emphasize the significant improvements over Neurosynth.

7) In the Discussion, it would be very helpful to give readers some intuition for when NeuroQuery will not yield sensible results and when/how exactly it should be used (e.g., even a table of use cases that would be appropriate and inappropriate) – and how to interpret carefully (e.g., look at the semantic loadings, and if there is one anatomical term that dominates, realize that you're essentially getting a map for that brain region). The ADHD example is useful but doesn't really cover the space of principles/use cases. Here are some possible examples we have thought of:

A) Some particular limitations may arise from the predictive nature of neuroquery, which may be less intuitive to many readers. For example, if I put in "aphasia", I will get map for "language", because aphasia is semantically close to language. This is very sensible, but users should not, of course, take this as a map of "aphasia" to be related other terms and used in inference. Users might "discover" that aphasia patterns are very closely related to "language" patterns and make an inference about co-localization of healthy and abnormal function. Of course, it's not your responsibility to control all kinds of potential misuse. But pointers would be helpful to avoid another, e.g., "#cingulategate" (Lieberman et al., 2016 PNAS).

B) For example, let's consider again the case about "combination of mental processes that have been studied separately, but never together". From my understanding of the algorithm, suppose users query "auditory" + "working memory", basically the prediction will be a linear combination of activation maps from "auditory" and "working memory" (+ similar terms due to the smoothing/query expansion). As such, this assumes that compound mental processes yield activations that are linear combination of activation maps of individual mental processes. This should be made clear.

C) Playing around with NeuroQuery, there are some queries that generate obviously wrong results. For example, "autobiographical memory" should probably yield the default network, but we getting hippocampal/retrosplenial activation instead. This presumably happens because NeuroQuery "expanded" the query to become memory because "autobiographical memory" is not one of the 200 keywords? Interesting that NeuroSynth does get it correct (https://neurosynth.org/analyses/terms/autobiographical%20memory/).

D) Perhaps a brief discussion of other limitations would be helpful. We submit that some of the fundamental problems are those not easily solved – that we usually perform meta-analyses based on studies of the same nominal task type (e.g., N-back), and sometimes minor variations in task structure can yield divergent findings. We don't know what all the dimensions are yet. This problem goes far beyond the challenge of establishing a set of consensus labels for task types and relevant cognitive processes. In short, we don't really even know what task features to label yet in many cases, and they don't combine additively. A stop-signal task with one adaptive random walk may be different than one with four, as it allows a different type of cognitive strategy.

E) When to use it: For common terms, meta-analysis (e.g., Neurosynth) does very well (e.g., Figure 4). When would the authors recommend using NeuroQuery over another meta-analytic tool? Maybe they could provide a summary of use cases and conditions (e.g., when few studies of a term/topic are available). Also see point (C).

8) Discussion of other approaches: We submit that the field has become tracked into a relatively narrow space of the possible options and techniques for meta-analysis, based on local analysis of coordinates in MKDA/ALE. Alternatives could be mentioned as potential future directions. For example, early work explored clustering of spatial locations and spatial discriminant tests (e.g., Wager et al., 2002, 2004, 2005), and later work has explored spatial models (e.g., Kang, 2011, Kang, 2014, Wager, 2015) and more advanced co-activation models (Xue, 2014). While this is obviously beyond the scope of the present paper, future work might consider models of spatial co-activation when generating predictions and inferences about meta-analytic maps.

9) The methods are a bit unclear:

A) Significant details about methodologies are missing. How are term frequency and inverse document frequency computed?

B) Equation 5: How is σ^ij computed? Square root of the entries of equation 8?

C) Equation 5: What is the difference between σ^i and σ^ij? σ^i is a column/row of σ^ij?

D) Yj is the j-th column not i-th column of Y?

E) M is a v x n matrix, so equation 8 is a v x v matrix? We are confused how this maps to σ^ij.

F) In Equation 10, is ||U||_1 just the sum of absolute values of all entries in U?

G) What is k set to be in equation 10?

H) "More than 72% of the time, NeuroQuery's output has a higher Pearson correlation with the correct map than with the negative example" – "correct map" refers to the KDE density maps?

10) Subsection “Smoothing: regularization at test time” is hard to read. It would be helpful if the authors explain the intuition behind the different steps and what the different matrices represent. For example, it might be helpful to explain that each row of V can be thought of as the association of words with topic k, so a higher value for row i, column j suggests the j-th dictionary word is more strongly related to the topic k. As another example, the authors should also unpack subsection “Smoothing: regularization at test time”: why do we take V and scale with 𝑛𝑖,𝑖 and then compute C and then l1-normalizing the rows of C to produce T and then finally S. What does each step try to do? We guess roughly speaking VV^T is like a co-occurrence matrix (how likely are two words likely to appear together?), but we are not sure why we have to do the extra normalization with 𝑛𝑖,𝑖, l1-normalization, etc.

claims.source: Thus, it makes better use of the available information, and can recover biologically plausible brain maps where other automated methods lack statistical power, for example with terms that are used in few studies, as shown in Section 'NeuroQuery can map rare or difficult concepts'.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by results presented in a later section of the manuscript.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery is easily usable online at neuroquery.org.
claims.source: NeuroQuery is easily usable online, at neuroquery.org, and the data and source code can be freely downloaded.
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of the NeuroQuery tool.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery model uses an estimate of the relatedness of terms in the vocabulary derived from co-occurrence statistics.
claims.source: The main components of the NeuroQuery model are an estimate of the relatedness of terms in the vocabulary, derived from co-occurrence statistics, and a regression model that links term occurrences to neural activations using supervised machine learning techniques.
claims.evidence: This describes the components of the NeuroQuery statistical model.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery uses a linear regression model to transform term representations into brain maps.
claims.source: Then, it transforms the resulting representation into a brain map using a linear regression model (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology of NeuroQuery, illustrated in Figure 3.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery maps are predictions of the likelihood of observation brain location rescaled by their standard deviation.
claims.source: The maps it outputs are predictions of the likelihood of observation brain location (rescaled by their standard deviation).
claims.evidence: This describes the nature of the output from the NeuroQuery model.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery maps do not have the same meaning as ALE, MKDA or NeuroSynth maps as they do not show a voxel-level test statistic.
claims.source: They do not have the same meaning as ALE, MKDA or NeuroSynth maps as they do not show a voxel-level test statistic.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of NeuroQuery outputs with other meta-analysis methods.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery corpus contains 13,459 full-text neuroimaging publications.
claims.source: NeuroQuery relies on a corpus of 13459 full-text neuroimaging publications, described in Section 'Building the NeuroQuery training data'.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the size of the corpus used.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery corpus is the largest of its kind.
claims.source: This corpus is by far the largest of its kind; the NeuroSynth corpus contains a similar number of documents, but uses only the article abstracts, and not the full article texts.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative claim about corpus size, which can be verified by comparing with other available corpora.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery represents the text of a document with Term Frequency · Inverse Document Frequency (TFIDF) features.
claims.source: We represent the text of a document with the (weighted) occurrence frequencies of each phrase from a fixed vocabulary, that is Term Frequency · Inverse Document Frequency (TFIDF) features (Salton and Buckley, 1988).
claims.evidence: This describes the text representation method used in NeuroQuery, with citation to the original TFIDF paper.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery vocabulary comprises 7,547 terms or phrases related to neuroscience that occur in at least 0.05% of publications.
claims.source: It comprises 7547 terms or phrases related to neuroscience that occur in at least 0.05% of publications.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the vocabulary size and selection criteria.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery automatically extracts 418,772 peak activation coordinates from publications.
claims.source: We automatically extract 418772 peak activations coordinates from publications, and transform them to brain maps with a kernel density estimator.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the coordinate extraction process and the number of coordinates extracted.

claims.claim: Term co-occurrences are more consistent and reliable than peak activation coordinates and capture semantic relationships.
claims.source: Term co-occurrences, on the other hand, are more consistent and reliable, and capture semantic relationships (Turney and Pantel, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turney and Pantel, 2010.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery uses Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to compute a low-rank approximation of word co-occurrences.
claims.source: Using Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), we compute a low-rank approximation of word co-occurrences (the covariance of the TFIDF features), and obtain a denoised semantic relatedness matrix (details are provided in Section 'smoothing: regularization at test time').
claims.evidence: This describes the method used for semantic smoothing in NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery's text-to-brain encoding model uses linear regression to map text onto brain activations.
claims.source: When analyzing the literature, we fit a linear regression to reliably map text onto brain activations.
claims.evidence: This describes the regression approach used in NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery's model is an additive one across term occurrences.
claims.source: This model is an additive one across the term occurrences, as opposed to logical operations traditionally used to select studies for meta-analysis.
claims.evidence: This describes the modeling approach and contrasts it with traditional methods.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery uses a reweighted ridge regression and feature selection procedure to prevent uninformative terms from degrading performance.
claims.source: We use a reweighted ridge regression and feature selection procedure (described in Section 'reweighted ridge matrix and feature (vocabulary) selection') to prevent uninformative terms such as 'magnetoencephalography' from degrading performance.
claims.evidence: This describes the regularization approach used in NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: The feature selection procedure automatically selects around 200 keywords that display a strong statistical link with brain activity.
claims.source: This procedure automatically selects around 200 keywords that display a strong statistical link with brain activity and adapts the regularization applied to each feature.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the outcome of the feature selection procedure.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery reports a map of Z statistics.
claims.source: In addition, NeuroQuery uses an estimate of the voxel-level variance of association (see methodological details in Section 'Mathematical details of the NeuroQuery statistical model'), and reports a map of Z statistics.
claims.evidence: This describes the output format of NeuroQuery predictions.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery maps cannot be thresholded to reject any simple null hypothesis.
claims.source: Therefore, the resulting map cannot be thresholded to reject any simple null hypothesis.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the statistical interpretation of NeuroQuery maps.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery maps have a different meaning and different uses than standard meta-analysis maps obtained with ALE.
claims.source: NeuroQuery maps have a different meaning and different uses than standard meta-analysis maps obtained e.g. with ALE.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative statement about the interpretation of different types of meta-analysis maps.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery can obtain a brain map directly from a contrast description without manual intervention.
claims.source: The NeuroQuery map was obtained directly from the contrast description in the dataset's documentation, without needing to manually select studies for the meta-analysis nor convert this description to a string pattern usable by existing automatic meta-analysis tools.
claims.evidence: This describes the capability of NeuroQuery as demonstrated in Figure 2.

claims.claim: With only 29 matching studies, ALE lacks statistical power for the contrast description 'Read pseudo-words vs. consonant strings'.
claims.source: With only 29 matching studies, ALE lacks statistical power for this contrast description.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of ALE for this specific query, based on the number of matching studies.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery can give good brain maps on combinations of terms that have never been studied together.
claims.source: To study the predictions of NeuroQuery, we first demonstrate that it can indeed give good brain maps on combinations of terms that have never been studied together.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The extrapolation from two terms to their combination is possible thanks to the linear additive model.
claims.source: The extrapolation from two terms for which the model has seen studies, 'distance' and 'color', to their combination, for which the model has no data, is possible thanks to the linear additive model, combining regression maps for 'distance' and 'color'.
claims.evidence: This explains the mechanism by which NeuroQuery can generalize to unseen term combinations.

claims.claim: Measures of how well predictions match the literature decrease only slightly for studies with terms already seen together compared to studies with terms never seen jointly.
claims.source: We find that measures of how well predictions match the literature decrease only slightly for studies with terms already seen together compared to studies with terms never seen jointly (details in Section 'NeuroQuery performance on unseen pairs of terms').
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experiments on unseen term pairs.

claims.claim: For 1,000 pairs of terms, the median correlation between the predicted map for the unseen combination and the meta-analytic map obtained on left-out studies is 0.85.
claims.source: We find a median correlation of 0.85 which shows that the excellent performance observed on Figure 4 is not due to a specific choice of terms.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments on unseen term pairs.

claims.claim: GCLDA is the only multivariate meta-analytic model to date.
claims.source: GCLDA is an important baseline because it is the only multivariate meta-analytic model to date.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the uniqueness of GCLDA in the field of meta-analysis.

claims.claim: GCLDA produces maps with low spatial resolution because it models brain activations as a mixture of Gaussians.
claims.source: However, it produces maps with a low spatial resolution because it models brain activations as a mixture of Gaussians.
claims.evidence: This is a characterization of GCLDA's limitations based on its modeling approach.

claims.claim: GCLDA takes several days to train and a dozen seconds to produce a map at test time.
claims.source: Moreover, it takes several days to train and a dozen of seconds to produce a map at test time, and is thus unsuitable to build an online and responsive tool like NeuroSynth or NeuroQuery.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the computational requirements of GCLDA.

claims.claim: By combining term similarities and an additive encoding model, NeuroQuery can accurately map rare or difficult terms for which standard meta-analysis lacks statistical power.
claims.source: By combining term similarities and an additive encoding model, NeuroQuery can accurately map rare or difficult terms for which standard meta-analysis lacks statistical power, as visible on Figure 5.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by results shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: Document frequencies roughly follow a power law, meaning that most words are very rare.
claims.source: Document frequencies roughly follow a power law (Piantadosi, 2014), meaning that most words are very rare – half the terms in our vocabulary occur in less than 76 articles (see Section 'Word occurrence frequencies across the corpus').
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Piantadosi, 2014 and data about term frequencies in the corpus.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery only needs a dozen examples to produce maps that are qualitatively and quantitatively close to the maps it obtains for the full corpus for many terms.
claims.source: For many terms, NeuroQuery only needs a dozen examples to produce maps that are qualitatively and quantitatively close to the maps it obtains for the full corpus – and to NeuroSynth's full-corpus maps.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experiments shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: NeuroSynth typically needs hundreds of examples to obtain results similar to those from the full corpus.
claims.source: NeuroSynth typically needs hundreds of examples to obtain similar results, as seen in Figure 6.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by results shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Reducing the number of studies required to map well a term greatly widens the vocabulary that can be studied by meta-analysis.
claims.source: Reducing the number of studies required to map well a term (a.k.a. the sample complexity of the meta-analysis model) therefore greatly widens the vocabulary that can be studied by meta-analysis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that most terms are rare and NeuroQuery requires fewer examples.

claims.claim: Capturing relations between terms is important because the literature does not use a perfectly consistent terminology.
claims.source: Capturing relations between terms is important because the literature does not use a perfectly consistent terminology.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the importance of semantic modeling based on observed variability in terminology.

claims.claim: Controlled vocabularies tend to have low coverage.
claims.source: The standard solution is to use expert-built ontologies (Poldrack and Yarkoni, 2016), but these tend to have low coverage.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation and by data shown in Table 1.

claims.claim: Ontologies are typically incomplete in listing relations across terms.
claims.source: In addition, ontologies are typically even more incomplete in listing relations across terms.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about limitations of ontologies based on general knowledge of their construction.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery relies on distributional semantics and co-occurrence statistics across the literature to estimate relatedness between terms.
claims.source: Rather than ontologies, NeuroQuery relies on distributional semantics and co-occurrence statistics across the literature to estimate relatedness between terms.
claims.evidence: This describes the approach used in NeuroQuery for modeling semantic relationships.

claims.claim: Continuous semantic links provide robustness to inconsistent terminology.
claims.source: These continuous semantic links provide robustness to inconsistent terminology: consistent meta-analytic maps for similar terms.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the benefit of the semantic smoothing approach, supported by examples in Figure 1.

claims.claim: Working with the full text of publications associates many more studies to a query than using abstracts.
claims.source: Another reason is that working with the full text of publications associates many more studies to a query: 2779 for 'color', while NeuroSynth matches only 236 abstracts, and 147 for 'huntington', a term not known to NeuroSynth.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of study matching between full-text and abstract-based approaches.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery is a predictive model that can produce brain maps for out-of-sample neuroimaging studies.
claims.source: Unlike standard meta-analysis methods, which compute in-sample summary statistics, NeuroQuery is a predictive model, that can produce brain maps for out-of-sample neuroimaging studies.
claims.evidence: This describes the nature of NeuroQuery as a predictive model.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery captures reliable links from concepts to brain activity that generalize to new, unseen neuroimaging studies.
claims.source: Here we check that NeuroQuery captures reliable links from concepts to brain activity – associations that generalize to new, unseen neuroimaging studies.
claims.evidence: This claim is evaluated through cross-validation experiments described in the manuscript.

claims.claim: NeuroSynth does not perform well for encoding full documents because it is designed for single-phrase meta-analysis.
claims.source: NeuroSynth does not perform well for this test. Indeed, the NeuroSynth model is designed for single-phrase meta-analysis, and does not have a mechanism to combine words and encode a full document.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of NeuroSynth based on its design.

claims.claim: GCLDA performs significantly better than chance but worse than a simple ridge regression baseline.
claims.source: GCLDA performs significantly better than chance, but still worse than a simple ridge regression baseline.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative performance claim based on experiments shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: More than 72% of the time, NeuroQuery's output has a higher Pearson correlation with the correct map than with a negative example.
claims.source: More than 72% of the time, NeuroQuery's output has a higher Pearson correlation with the correct map than with the negative example (see Figure 7 right).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from the encoding prediction experiment.

claims.claim: Peak coordinates reported in the literature are noisy and incomplete with respect to the full activation maps.
claims.source: However, the scores are difficult to interpret, as peak coordinates reported in the literature are noisy and incomplete with respect to the full activation maps.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of using peak coordinates as ground truth.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery predictions match well the IBMA results, with a median Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.80.
claims.source: NeuroQuery predictions match well the IBMA results, with a median Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.80.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with BrainPedia IBMA maps.

claims.claim: Manually reformulating the labels to terms from NeuroSynth's vocabulary gives a median AUC of 0.83 for NeuroSynth and 0.88 for NeuroQuery.
claims.source: Manually reformulating the labels to terms from NeuroSynth's vocabulary gives a median AUC of .83 for NeuroSynth, and also raises the AUC to .88 for NeuroQuery (details in Section 'Comparison with the BrainPedia IBMA study' and Figure 13).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with BrainPedia IBMA maps using reformulated labels.

claims.claim: Both NeuroSynth and NeuroQuery produce maps that are close to the Harvard-Oxford anatomical atlas regions, with a median AUC of 0.98 for NeuroQuery and 0.95 for NeuroSynth.
claims.source: Both NeuroSynth and NeuroQuery produce maps that are close to the atlases' manually segmented regions, with a median AUC of 0.98 for NeuroQuery and 0.95 for NeuroSynth, for the region labels that are present in NeuroSynth's vocabulary.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with anatomical atlas regions.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth maps for well-captured terms are very similar, with a median AUC of 0.90.
claims.source: We compare NeuroQuery predictions to NeuroSynth activations by computing the AUC. NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth maps for these well-captured terms are very similar, with a median AUC of 0.90.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from comparison with NeuroSynth on terms with strong activations.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery is available as an open-source Python package that can be easily installed on all platforms.
claims.source: NeuroQuery is also available as an open-source Python package that can be easily installed on all platforms: https://github.com/neuroquery/neuroquery (copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/neuroquery).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about the availability of the NeuroQuery software.

claims.claim: All the resources used to build NeuroQuery are freely available at https://github.com/neuroquery/neuroquery_data.
claims.source: Finally, all the resources used to build NeuroQuery are freely available at https://github.com/neuroquery/neuroquery_data (copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/neuroquery_data).
claims.evidence: This is a factual statement about data availability.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery corpus is significantly richer than NeuroSynth.
claims.source: The corpus is significantly richer than NeuroSynth, the largest corpus to date (see Table 3 for a comparison), and manual quality assurance reveals more accurate extraction of brain coordinates (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparisons shown in Tables 2 and 3.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery departs from existing meta-analytic frameworks by treating meta-analysis as a prediction problem.
claims.source: For this, it departs from existing meta-analytic frameworks by treating meta-analysis as a prediction problem.
claims.evidence: This describes the conceptual difference between NeuroQuery and traditional meta-analysis.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery describes neuroscience concepts of interest by continuous combinations of terms rather than matching publications for exact terms.
claims.source: It describes neuroscience concepts of interest by continuous combinations of terms rather than matching publications for exact terms.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological approach of NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery extends the scope of meta-analysis in neuroimaging by combining multiple terms and interpolating between available studies.
claims.source: As it combines multiple terms and interpolates between available studies, it extends the scope of meta-analysis in neuroimaging.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the capabilities of NeuroQuery compared to traditional methods.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery can capture information for concepts studied much less frequently than those covered by current automated meta-analytic approaches.
claims.source: In particular, it can capture information for concepts studied much less frequently than those that are covered by current automated meta-analytic approaches.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experiments on rare terms shown in the results section.

claims.claim: Brainmap was the first systematic database of brain coordinates.
claims.source: Brainmap (Laird et al., 2005) was the first systematic database of brain coordinates.
claims.evidence: This is a historical statement about Brainmap, supported by citation.

claims.claim: NeuroSynth pioneered automated meta-analysis using abstracts from the literature.
claims.source: NeuroSynth (Yarkoni et al., 2011) pioneered automated meta-analysis using abstracts from the literature, broadening a lot the set of terms for which the consistency of reported locations can be tested.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about NeuroSynth's contribution to the field, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Nielsen et al. (2004) used non-negative matrix factorization on the matrix of occurrences of terms for each brain location to extract seven spatial networks associated with cognitive topics.
claims.source: Nielsen et al. (2004) used a non-negative matrix factorization on the matrix of occurrences of terms for each brain location (voxel): their model outputs a set of seven spatial networks associated with cognitive topics, described as weighted combinations of terms.
claims.evidence: This describes prior work by Nielsen et al., supported by citation.

claims.claim: Poldrack et al. (2012) used topic models on the full text of 5,800 publications to extract 130 topics on mental function and disorders.
claims.source: Poldrack et al. (2012) used topic models on the full text of 5800 publications to extract from term cooccurrences 130 topics on mental function and disorders, followed by a classic meta-analysis to map their neural correlates in the literature.
claims.evidence: This describes prior work by Poldrack et al., supported by citation.

claims.claim: The supervised learning used in NeuroQuery differs from that used in Yarkoni et al. (2011) as the latter is a decoding model.
claims.source: In this sense, the supervised learning used in NeuroQuery differs from that used in Yarkoni et al. (2011) : the latter is a decoding model that, given brain locations in a study, predicts the likelihood of neuroscience terms without using relationships between terms.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of NeuroQuery with prior work, supported by citation.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery will be most successfully used to produce hypotheses and as an exploratory tool.
claims.source: Rather, NeuroQuery will be most successfully used to produce hypotheses and as an exploratory tool, to be confronted with other sources of evidence.
claims.evidence: This is a recommendation about how to use NeuroQuery based on its design and limitations.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery does not provide conclusive evidence that a brain region is recruited by a mental process or affected by a pathology.
claims.source: What NeuroQuery does not do is provide conclusive evidence that a brain region is recruited by a mental process or affected by a pathology.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery is particularly beneficial when the term of interest is rare, when the concept is best described by multiple terms, and when a fully automated method is necessary.
claims.source: Compared to traditional meta-analysis tools, NeuroQuery is particularly beneficial (i) when the term of interest is rare, (ii) when the concept of interest is best described by a combination of multiple terms, and (iii) when a fully automated method is necessary and queries would otherwise need cumbersome manual curation to be understood by other tools.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the use cases where NeuroQuery provides advantages.

claims.claim: For 'agnosia', the NeuroQuery prediction is driven by indirect associations and focuses on the visual system.
claims.source: In this specific case, the indirect association is problematic because 'agnosia' is not a selected term that NeuroQuery can map by itself, as it is not well-represented in the source data. As a result, the NeuroQuery prediction for 'agnosia' is driven by indirect associations, and focuses on the visual system, rather than areas related to, for example auditory agnosia.
claims.evidence: This is an example of a limitation of NeuroQuery for a specific term.

claims.claim: For 'ADHD', the model builds its prediction on terms that are distant from the query and produces a misleading map.
claims.source: Hence, for 'ADHD', the model builds its prediction on terms that are distant from the query, and produces a misleading map that highlights mostly the cerebellum (https://neuroquery.org/query?text=adhd).
claims.evidence: This is an example of a failure case for NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery interface reports failures with a warning stating that results may not be reliable.
claims.source: While this result is not satisfying, the failure is detected by the NeuroQuery interface and reported with a warning stating that results may not be reliable.
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the NeuroQuery interface for handling failure cases.

claims.claim: The additive combination model is not unique to NeuroQuery and lies at the heart of functional neuroimaging.
claims.source: This model is not unique to NeuroQuery, and lies at the heart of functional neuroimaging, which builds upon the hypothesis of pure insertion of cognitive processes (Ulrich et al., 1999; Poldrack, 2010).
claims.evidence: This contextualizes the additive model used in NeuroQuery within the broader field, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Meta-analyses have little or no ability to correct biases present in the primary literature.
claims.source: First, meta-analyses have little or no ability to correct biases present in the primary literature (e.g., perhaps confirmation bias drives researchers to overreport amygdala activation in emotion studies).
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about limitations of meta-analysis.

claims.claim: Claims that a structure is selective to a mental condition need an explicit statistical model of reverse inference.
claims.source: However, claims that a structure is selective to a mental condition need an explicit statistical model of reverse inference (Wager et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about requirements for making selectivity claims, supported by citation.

claims.claim: The most important confound for reverse inferences in meta-analysis is that some brain locations are reported for many different conditions.
claims.source: In a meta-analysis, the most important confound for reverse inferences is that some brain locations are reported for many different conditions.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about a methodological challenge in meta-analysis.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery accounts for varying baseline across the brain by fitting an intercept and reporting only differences from the baseline.
claims.source: NeuroQuery accounts for this varying baseline across the brain by fitting an intercept and reporting only differences from the baseline.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological feature of NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: Minor variations in task design for finger tapping lead to reproducible variations in neural responses.
claims.source: Indeed, even for a task as simple as finger tapping, minor variations in task design lead to reproducible variations in neural responses (Witt et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Witt et al., 2008.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery grounds meta-analysis in the full-text descriptions of the studies.
claims.source: Rather, NeuroQuery grounds meta-analysis in the full-text descriptions of the studies, which in our view provide the best available proxy for such an idealized ontology.
claims.evidence: This describes the approach taken by NeuroQuery to handle the lack of a complete ontology.

claims.claim: NeuroSynth took a huge step by enabling anyone to perform a fully automated meta-analysis across thousands of studies in a few seconds.
claims.source: NeuroSynth took a huge step in this direction by enabling anyone to perform, in a few seconds, a fully automated meta-analysis across thousands of studies, for an important number of isolated terms.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of NeuroSynth to the field.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery provides statistical maps for arbitrary queries from seldom-studied terms to free-text descriptions of experimental protocols.
claims.source: NeuroQuery provides statistical maps for arbitrary queries – from seldom-studied terms to free-text descriptions of experimental protocols.
claims.evidence: This describes the capabilities of NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery enables applying fully-automated and quantitative meta-analysis in situations where only semi-manual and subjective solutions were available.
claims.source: Thus, it enables applying fully-automated and quantitative meta-analysis in situations where only semi-manual and subjective solutions were available.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the advancement provided by NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery dataset was collected by downloading around 149,000 full-text journal articles from PubMed Central and Elsevier APIs.
claims.source: We downloaded around 149000 full-text journal articles related to neuroimaging from the PubMed Central (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/, https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK25501/) (Sayers, 2009) and Elsevier (https://dev.elsevier.com/api_docs.html) APIs.
claims.evidence: This describes the data collection process for NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery dataset contains studies mostly based on fMRI experiments, but also includes PET or structural MRI studies.
claims.source: The resulting studies are mostly based on fMRI experiments, but the dataset also contains Positron Emission Tomography (PET) or structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) studies.
claims.evidence: This describes the composition of the NeuroQuery dataset.

claims.claim: Out of 149,000 downloaded and formatted articles, 13,459 contain coordinates that could be extracted.
claims.source: Out of the 149000 downloaded and formatted articles, 13459 contain coordinates that could be extracted by this process, resulting in a total of 418772 locations.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the coordinate extraction results.

claims.claim: All extracted coordinates are treated as coordinates in the MNI space, even though some articles refer to the Talairach space.
claims.source: All the extracted coordinates are treated as coordinates in the Montreal Neurological Institute (MNI) space, even though some articles still refer to the Talairach space.
claims.evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the coordinate extraction process.

claims.claim: Differences between the Talairach and MNI coordinate systems are at most of the order of 1 cm.
claims.source: However, differences between the two coordinate systems are at most of the order of 1 cm, and much smaller in most of the brain.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the magnitude of differences between coordinate systems.

claims.claim: Out of 8,692 articles in the intersection of NeuroSynth and NeuroQuery corpora, the extracted coordinates differ in 1,961 articles (23%).
claims.source: Out of 8692 articles in the intersection of both corpora, the extracted coordinates differ (for at least one coordinate) in 1961 (i.e. in 23% of articles).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of coordinate extraction between NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery's coordinate extraction method extracted false coordinates from 3 out of 40 manually annotated articles, compared to 20 for NeuroSynth.
claims.source: As shown in Table 2, our method extracted false coordinates from fewer articles: 3/40 articles have at least one false location in our dataset, against 20 for NeuroSynth.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative result from manual evaluation of coordinate extraction.

claims.claim: NeuroQuery uses Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation with a bandwidth yielding a FWHM close to 9 mm.
claims.source: We then use Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 2015) to estimate the density of these activations over the brain. The chosen bandwidth of the Gaussian kernel yields a Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) close to 9 mm, which is in the range of smoothing kernels that are typically used for fMRI meta-analysis (Wager et al., 2007; Wager et al., 2004; Turkeltaub et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This describes the density estimation method used in NeuroQuery, with citations to relevant literature.

claims.claim: NeuroSynth uses a hard ball of 10 mm radius for density estimation.
claims.source: For comparison, NeuroSynth uses a hard ball of 10 mm radius.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of density estimation methods between NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery vocabulary is built from the union of terms from several ontologies and labels from 12 anatomical atlases.
claims.source: This vocabulary is built from the union of terms from several ontologies (shown in Table 1) and labels from 12 anatomical atlases (listed in Table 4 in Section 'The choice of vocabulary').
claims.evidence: This describes the sources used to construct the NeuroQuery vocabulary.

claims.claim: TFIDF representations are simple and efficient for many text classification and retrieval applications.
claims.source: These simple representations are popular in document retrieval and text classification because they are very efficient for many applications.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the utility of TFIDF features based on general knowledge in natural language processing.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery corpus contains over 418,000 peak activation coordinates for more than 13,500 articles.
claims.source: Over 418K peak activation coordinates for more than 13.5K articles.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statistic about the NeuroQuery dataset.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery vocabulary contains 7,547 terms related to neuroscience, each occurring in at least six articles from which coordinates were extracted.
claims.source: A vocabulary of 7547 terms related to neuroscience, each occurring in at least six articles from which we extracted coordinates.
claims.evidence: This describes the vocabulary used in NeuroQuery.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery dataset is the largest of its kind.
claims.source: This dataset is the largest of its kind.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative claim about the size of the NeuroQuery dataset.

claims.claim: In terms of raw amount of text, the NeuroQuery corpus is 20 times larger than NeuroSynth's.
claims.source: In terms of raw amount of text, this corpus is 20 times larger than NeuroSynth's.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of corpus sizes.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery corpus yields over 5.5 million occurrences of a unique term in an article, over five times more than NeuroSynth.
claims.source: Combined with our vocabulary, it yields over 5.5M occurrences of a unique term in an article. This is over five times more than the word occurrence counts distributed by NeuroSynth (https://github.com/neurosynth/neurosynth-data).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of term-study associations.

claims.claim: When considering only terms in NeuroSynth's vocabulary, the NeuroQuery corpus contains over 3 million term-study associations, 4.6 times more than NeuroSynth.
claims.source: When considering only terms in NeuroSynth's vocabulary, the corpus still contains over 3M term-study associations, 4.6 times more than NeuroSynth.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison controlling for vocabulary differences.

claims.claim: There is an important overlap between NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth datasets: 8,692 studies are present in both.
claims.source: There is an important overlap between the selected studies: 8 692 studies are present in both datasets – the Intersection Over Union is 0.45.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative measure of dataset overlap.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery coordinate extraction set is almost the size of NeuroSynth's, which is 7% larger with 448,255 coordinates.

claims.claim: Compared with NeuroSynth, NeuroQuery's extraction method reduced the number of articles with incorrect coordinates by a factor of 7.
claims.source: Compared with NeuroSynth, NeuroQuery's extraction method reduced the number of articles with incorrect coordinates (false positives) by a factor of 7, and the number of articles with missing coordinates (false negatives) by a factor of 3 (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of coordinate extraction accuracy.

claims.claim: The most informative words in ridge regression are associated with large coefficients for many voxels.
claims.source: Our approach is based on the observation that when fitting a ridge regression with a uniform regularization, the most informative words are associated with large coefficients for many voxels.
claims.evidence: This is an observation that motivates the feature selection approach.

claims.claim: The feature selection has a very low computational cost compared to other feature selection schemes.
claims.source: It has a very low computational cost compared to other feature selection schemes.

claims.claim: The NeuroQuery model is not very sensitive to the NMF hyperparameters.

results.result: NeuroQuery is built on a large corpus of 13,459 full-text neuroimaging publications with 418,772 extracted peak activation coordinates and a vocabulary of 7,547 neuroscience terms. This corpus is significantly larger and richer than existing resources like NeuroSynth, containing 20 times more text and over 5 times more term-study associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C26-C30, C98-C117, and C72 collectively establish the size and composition of the NeuroQuery dataset with specific quantitative metrics. The comparisons with NeuroSynth are supported by Table 3, and the coordinate extraction quality is validated through manual annotation (Table 2). The claims are internally consistent and provide converging evidence for the dataset's scale and quality.

results.result: NeuroQuery uses a multivariate predictive model that combines semantic smoothing via NMF with supervised ridge regression to map arbitrary text queries to brain activation patterns. The model is trained on 13,459 publications using TFIDF features and automatically selects approximately 200 keywords with strong links to brain activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C12, C16-C18, C22-C23, C28, C32-C36, C73-C74 describe the core statistical methodology of NeuroQuery. The approach is clearly documented with mathematical details provided in the Methods section. The two-stage process (semantic smoothing followed by regression) is well-justified and the feature selection procedure is quantitatively described. Figure 3 provides visual illustration of the pipeline.

results.result: NeuroQuery can accurately predict brain maps for unseen combinations of terms that have never been studied together, achieving a median correlation of 0.85 between predicted maps and meta-analytic maps from left-out studies containing those term combinations.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by systematic experiments on 1,000 randomly chosen term pairs (Figure 4, Figure 9, Figure 10). The quantitative results show only slight decreases in performance for unseen term pairs compared to standard cross-validation, and the median Pearson correlation of 0.85 demonstrates strong generalization. The linear additive model mechanism is clearly explained.

results.result: NeuroQuery requires far fewer examples than existing methods to produce accurate brain maps for rare terms. For many terms, NeuroQuery needs only a dozen examples to produce maps close to full-corpus results, while NeuroSynth typically needs hundreds of examples.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C53 and C76 are supported by systematic subsampling experiments shown in Figure 6. The power law distribution of term frequencies (C50, supported by citation and Figure 16) establishes why this capability is important. The quantitative comparison between NeuroQuery and NeuroSynth convergence rates provides clear evidence for the reduced sample complexity.

results.result: NeuroQuery is a predictive model that generalizes to out-of-sample studies, outperforming GCLDA, ridge regression baselines, and NeuroSynth on encoding prediction tasks. NeuroQuery achieves >72% accuracy in matching publications to their brain maps and shows significantly better log-likelihood of reported coordinates.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C64 are supported by 16-fold cross-validation experiments (Figure 7). The quantitative metrics (log-likelihood and pairwise matching) provide clear evidence of predictive performance. The comparison with baselines is appropriate, though the explanation for NeuroSynth's poor performance (C62) is reasonable given its design for single-phrase meta-analysis rather than full-document encoding.

results.result: NeuroQuery predictions closely match reference meta-analytic maps and anatomical atlases, achieving median AUCs of 0.80-0.88 for IBMA maps, 0.98 for Harvard-Oxford atlas regions, and 0.90 for NeuroSynth maps on well-captured terms.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 are supported by systematic comparisons with multiple reference standards (Figures 13-15). The AUC metrics provide quantitative validation against high-quality ground truth. The improvement when reformulating labels (C67) demonstrates the importance of vocabulary matching. The high agreement with anatomical atlases (C68) provides strong validation for anatomical terms.

results.result: NeuroQuery addresses the problem of inconsistent terminology in neuroscience by using distributional semantics and co-occurrence statistics rather than expert-built ontologies, providing robustness to terminology variations through continuous semantic links.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C54-C58 are supported by Figure 1 showing consistent maps for related terms, Table 1 demonstrating low vocabulary overlap across ontologies, and the semantic smoothing methodology described in the Methods. The approach is well-justified given the documented limitations of existing ontologies (low coverage and incomplete relations).

results.result: NeuroQuery can generate brain maps directly from contrast descriptions without manual study selection, as demonstrated for the IBC dataset contrast 'Read pseudo-words vs. consonant strings', where ALE with only 29 matching studies lacks statistical power.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by Figure 2 and Figure 8, which show the NeuroQuery map overlaid on the actual IBC group-level map and compare it to the underpowered ALE result. The demonstration is compelling, though it represents a single case study. The claim about ALE lacking power with 29 studies is reasonable but could benefit from more formal statistical justification.

results.result: Only 30% of terms in neuroscience ontologies or meta-analysis tools are common across resources, and the lack of a universally established vocabulary is a strong impediment to meta-analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C11 are directly supported by Table 1, which quantitatively demonstrates the low overlap between major neuroscience vocabularies. The citation to Poldrack and Yarkoni (2016) provides additional support. The data clearly shows that most pairwise overlaps are well below 30%, with many below 10%.

results.result: NeuroQuery's coordinate extraction method is more accurate than NeuroSynth's, reducing false positives by a factor of 7 and false negatives by a factor of 3 based on manual annotation of 40 articles.
results.evaluation: Claims C104 and C117 are supported by Table 2, which presents results from manual annotation of 40 articles where the two extraction methods disagreed. However, the sample size is relatively small (40 articles from a subset where methods disagree), and the authors acknowledge that errors are less likely in articles where both methods agree. The results are suggestive but limited in scope.

results.result: NeuroQuery maps are predictions of likelihood of observation rescaled by standard deviation and reported as Z statistics, but they do not control a voxel-level null hypothesis and have different meaning than ALE, MKDA, or NeuroSynth maps.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C25, C37-C39, and C15 accurately describe the statistical nature of NeuroQuery outputs and their differences from traditional meta-analysis. This is an important limitation that is clearly stated. The distinction between predictive maps and hypothesis-testing maps is conceptually sound and well-explained in the Methods section.

results.result: NeuroQuery is best used as an exploratory tool for hypothesis generation, ROI definition, and literature review rather than for providing conclusive evidence. It is particularly beneficial for rare terms, multi-term concepts, and fully automated queries.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 provide appropriate usage recommendations based on the tool's design and limitations. These recommendations are consistent with the statistical properties described in other claims (particularly C38-C39). The guidance is reasonable and helps users understand appropriate applications.

results.result: NeuroQuery has known failure modes for terms like 'agnosia' and 'ADHD' where predictions are driven by indirect or distant associations, but the interface detects and warns users about unreliable results.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 honestly describe specific failure cases with clear examples. The explanation of why these failures occur (terms not well-represented in source data, no closely related terms with strong brain activity links) is reasonable. The warning system in the interface is a good mitigation strategy. This transparent discussion of limitations strengthens the overall work.

results.result: Working with full text associates many more studies to a query than using abstracts: 2,779 studies for 'color' vs. 236 in NeuroSynth, and 147 for 'huntington' (not in NeuroSynth's vocabulary).
results.evaluation: Claim C59 provides specific quantitative examples of the benefit of using full text. These numbers are consistent with the overall corpus statistics (C112-C114) showing the NeuroQuery corpus contains 5+ times more term-study associations. The examples effectively illustrate the advantage of full-text analysis.

results.result: All extracted coordinates are treated as MNI coordinates even though some articles use Talairach space, which is acceptable because differences between the coordinate systems are at most ~1 cm and comparable to smoothing kernel size.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 describe a methodological choice that introduces some imprecision. While the justification that differences are small (~1 cm) and comparable to the smoothing kernel (9 mm FWHM) is reasonable, this is still a source of error. The authors acknowledge this could be improved. The claim about maximum differences being ~1 cm is stated as general knowledge without citation, though it is consistent with the literature (Lancaster et al., 2007 is cited for related context).

results.result: More than 6,000 publications per year contain 'neuroimaging' on PubMed, and individual brain-imaging studies seldom have enough statistical power to establish fully trustworthy results.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is a verifiable factual statement about PubMed publication counts. Claim C2 is supported by citations to Button et al., 2013 and Poldrack et al., 2017. These claims establish the motivation for meta-analysis but are background context rather than novel findings.

results.result: NeuroQuery is freely available as an online tool at neuroquery.org, as an open-source Python package, and all resources used to build it are freely available on GitHub.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 and C21 are factual statements about software and data availability that can be verified by visiting the provided URLs. This represents good open science practice and is important for reproducibility and adoption.

results.result: The additive combination model used by NeuroQuery is standard in functional neuroimaging based on pure insertion of cognitive processes. Meta-analyses have inherent limitations including inability to correct primary literature biases, and reverse inference requires explicit statistical modeling.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 provide important context about the assumptions and limitations of the approach and meta-analysis in general. These are supported by appropriate citations (Ulrich et al., 1999; Poldrack, 2010; Wager et al., 2016; Witt et al., 2008) and represent honest discussion of methodological constraints. C92 describes how NeuroQuery partially addresses baseline confounds.

results.result: GCLDA is the only multivariate meta-analytic model to date, but it produces low spatial resolution maps due to modeling activations as Gaussians and takes several days to train, making it unsuitable for online tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C48 characterize GCLDA as an important baseline. The statement about it being the only multivariate model (C46) is a strong claim about the field that could be challenged, but is presented as the authors' understanding. The limitations described (C47-C48) are reasonable characterizations based on the model's design and are supported by the performance comparisons in Figures 5-7.

results.result: Prior work including Brainmap, NeuroSynth, Nielsen et al. (2004), Poldrack et al. (2012), and Yarkoni et al. (2011) have contributed to automated meta-analysis and topic modeling in neuroimaging, with NeuroQuery differing by using supervised encoding rather than decoding models.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 provide appropriate context about related work, all supported by citations. The characterization of prior contributions appears accurate and the distinction between NeuroQuery's encoding approach and Yarkoni et al.'s decoding approach (C81) is clearly explained. This represents good scholarly practice in situating the work.

results.result: NeuroQuery uses Gaussian Kernel Density Estimation with bandwidth yielding FWHM close to 9 mm, which is in the typical range for fMRI meta-analysis, while NeuroSynth uses a hard ball of 10 mm radius.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C106 describe the density estimation methods with appropriate citations (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 2015; Wager et al., 2007; Wager et al., 2004; Turkeltaub et al., 2002). The choice of 9 mm FWHM is justified as being in the typical range. The comparison with NeuroSynth's approach is factual.

results.result: The feature selection procedure is based on the observation that informative words have large coefficients for many voxels in ridge regression, automatically selects approximately 200 features, and has very low computational cost.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121 describe the feature selection methodology. The observation in C119 is reasonable and motivates the approach. The outcome of ~200 features (C120) is consistent with C36. The claim about low computational cost (C121) is reasonable given it requires only two ridge regressions, though this is somewhat subjective without detailed timing comparisons.

results.result: The NeuroQuery model is not very sensitive to the NMF hyperparameters and obtains similar results for a range of different values.
results.evaluation: Claim C123 reports a robustness analysis of the NMF hyperparameters. While the specific values tested and results are not shown in detail, this type of sensitivity analysis is appropriate and the conclusion that the model is robust is stated clearly. More detailed results would strengthen this claim.

results.result: Current meta-analysis approaches model all studies as asking the same question. CBMA methods assess consistency by comparing spatial density of coordinates to uniform distribution, and NeuroSynth enables large-scale analyses with excellent statistical power.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C8-C9 characterize existing meta-analysis methods. C8 accurately describes CBMA with appropriate citations. C9's characterization of NeuroSynth is supported by citation. C4's claim that current approaches model all studies as asking the same question is a reasonable characterization of traditional meta-analysis that selects studies based on exact term matching, though it could be seen as somewhat oversimplified.

results.result: Peak coordinates reported in the literature are noisy and incomplete with respect to full activation maps, making prediction scores difficult to interpret.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is a reasonable statement about the limitations of using peak coordinates as ground truth for validation. This is general knowledge in the neuroimaging field and explains why the quantitative validation metrics (Figures 7, 9) should be interpreted with appropriate caution. The claim appropriately tempers interpretation of the results.

results.result: NeuroQuery can handle text of arbitrary length, considers terms in a contextually-informed way allowing mutual interactions, produces high-quality maps for infrequently studied concepts, and uses NLP techniques to infer semantic similarities.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C13-C14, C18-C20 describe capabilities of NeuroQuery that follow from its design. These are supported by the methodology (semantic smoothing + regression) and validated by the experiments on rare terms (Figures 5-6) and unseen combinations (Figure 4). The claims are consistent with the technical approach and empirical results.

results.result: Term co-occurrences are more consistent and reliable than peak activation coordinates and capture semantic relationships.
results.evaluation: Claim C31 is supported by citation to Turney and Pantel (2010) and is a well-established principle in natural language processing. This claim justifies the use of co-occurrence statistics for semantic smoothing in NeuroQuery. The principle is sound and appropriately applied.

results.result: NeuroQuery grounds meta-analysis in full-text descriptions as a proxy for an idealized ontology. It provides statistical maps for arbitrary queries and enables fully-automated meta-analysis where only semi-manual solutions were previously available.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 describe the conceptual approach and contribution of NeuroQuery. These are supported by the demonstrated capabilities (arbitrary text queries, rare terms, unseen combinations) and represent a reasonable characterization of the advancement over existing tools. The claim about enabling automation where manual curation was needed (C97) is supported by examples like Figure 2.

results.result: The NeuroQuery vocabulary is built from multiple ontologies and 12 anatomical atlases. TFIDF representations are simple and efficient for many text classification and retrieval applications.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 describes the vocabulary construction with reference to Table 1 and Table 4. Claim C108 is general knowledge about TFIDF features in NLP. Both claims are straightforward and well-supported.

results.result: Out of 8,692 articles in the intersection of NeuroSynth and NeuroQuery corpora, extracted coordinates differ in 1,961 articles (23%).
results.evaluation: Claim C103 provides a specific quantitative comparison of coordinate extraction between the two systems. This is a factual statement about the overlap analysis and sets up the manual validation study (C104). The 23% disagreement rate is substantial and motivates the quality comparison.
